summary: This Informational document describes how the LISP Mapping System can be spread across many parties for scale and managed in a decentralized way, while data plane nodes still trust it. It is meant to help LISP-Decent implementations interoperate.

plainLanguage.summary: One huge phone book run by one office is replaced by many offices sharing it, so no single office is a bottleneck.

subtitle: Decentralized mapping system where LISP nodes manage their own routing directories.

tldr.problem: LISP normally relies on a central Mapping System Provider to translate endpoint identifiers to routing locators, creating a single point of management and potential failure.
tldr.mechanism: LISP-Decent lets the routing nodes themselves act as map servers, sharing and maintaining mappings with each other either via multicast (push-based) or DNS plus hashing (pull-based).
tldr.outcome: The mapping system becomes distributed and decentralized, improving scalability and reducing dependence on third-party infrastructure.

today: RFC 9962 is an Informational RFC documenting a decentralized approach to LISP mapping systems. It does not mandate changes to LISP itself but provides guidance for implementations wishing to operate independent of a third-party Mapping System Provider. The approach is suitable for private deployments and organizations wanting full control over their mapping infrastructure.

sections.title: LISP and the Mapping System Problem
sections.content:
LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) is an overlay routing architecture that separates endpoint identifiers (EIDs) from routing locators (RLOCs). An EID is a stable address for a network site, while an RLOC is the actual IP address for reaching it. A Mapping System translates EIDs to RLOCs, similar to how DNS translates domain names to IP addresses.

Traditionally, the Mapping System is deployed and managed by a third-party Mapping System Provider (MSP) that runs map-servers and map-resolvers. LISP nodes (xTRs) depend on and trust this infrastructure but do not participate in managing it. This centralized model creates scalability challenges and operational dependencies. LISP-Decent solves this by making the xTRs themselves participate in maintaining the Mapping System.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP is like a system where everyone has two addresses: a stable home address and a current location. The mapping system is the directory that says where everyone currently is.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
A Decentralized Mapping System (DMS) is managed by the xTR nodes that use it rather than by third-party infrastructure. The xTRs themselves act as both clients (requesting mappings) and servers (providing mappings). This changes the trust model: instead of trusting an external MSP, nodes trust each other.

The document defines two approaches. A Decent-Push-based system uses IP multicast: all xTRs join the same multicast group and broadcast mappings to each other. A Decent-Pull-based system uses DNS and hashing: xTRs compute which map-server holds a particular mapping using a hash of the EID, then contact that server via DNS. The push model is simpler but requires multicast support; the pull model works over regular IP and uses less state per server.
sections.plainLanguage: Push-based is like everyone shouting their address to the whole group. Pull-based is like looking up someone's address in a phone book where the lookup uses a formula to find the right page.

sections.title: Push-Based Mapping with Multicast
sections.content:
In the Decent-Push-based approach, all participating xTRs join a single IP multicast group address, such as 233.252.1.1. When an xTR needs to register a mapping (e.g., my EID is 10.1.0.0/24 and it can be reached at RLOC 192.0.2.1), it sends a Map-Register message to the multicast group. All xTRs in the group receive and process the registration, maintaining synchronized state. When an ITR needs to lookup a mapping, it can send a Map-Request locally to its own map-resolver.

This approach requires only the LISP control-plane protocol; no additional transport protocols like LISP-ALT or LISP-DDT are needed. Adding or removing nodes from the group is straightforward. All servers hold all mappings, providing full redundancy. However, it requires the underlying network to support multicast, and a seed-group must be preconfigured to bootstrap the system.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone stands in a circle and announces their current address. If you want to find someone, you look in your local copy of the announcements.

sections.title: Pull-Based Mapping with DNS and Hashing
sections.content:
In the Decent-Pull-based approach, xTRs use a hash function and DNS to determine which map-server should hold a particular mapping. When an xTR wants to register or look up an EID, it hashes the EID (using SHA-256 over a formatted string like [iid]eid/prefix-length) and takes the hash modulo a configured Modulus Value. This produces an index (0 to N-1) that selects which DNS name to query.

For example, with Modulus Value 4, DNS names might be 0.map-server.example.com, 1.map-server.example.com, etc. Each DNS name has A and AAAA records pointing to the RLOCs of the map-servers responsible for that partition. Different servers hold different subsets of mappings, reducing per-server state. The pull model works without multicast and scales better for large numbers of servers, though it requires careful configuration to ensure all xTRs use the same hash algorithm and modulus value.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a formula to compute which person in the directory should keep a particular entry. Everyone uses the same formula so they all look in the same place.

sections.title: Hierarchical Organization and Seed-Groups
sections.content:
LISP-Decent supports a hierarchical organization where xTRs are organized into layers. A core seed-group contains the foundational nodes that bootstrap the system. Other xTRs can join additional mapping system groups to form new layers. Each layer registers its group addresses to the core seed-group, creating a multi-layer hierarchy.

This is useful for organizing xTRs geographically or by trust domain. For example, a core seed-group could bootstrap two regional mapping systems: one for inter-continental routes and one for intra-continental routes. Each regional group registers its group address to the core, making discovery possible through a chain of lookups.
sections.plainLanguage: You can have small address books for your local neighborhood and one big address book that knows about all the smaller ones.
